'''Paul Joseph Salomon Benacerraf''' ({{IPAc-en|ˌ|b|ɛ|n|ə|s|eɪ|ˈ|r|ɑː|f}}; 26 March 1930 – 13 January 2025) was a French-born American philosopher working in the field of the [[philosophy of mathematics]] who taught at [[Princeton University]] his entire career, from 1960 until his retirement in 2007. Benacerraf was appointed Stuart Professor of Philosophy in 1974, and retired as the James S. McDonnell Distinguished University Professor of Philosophy.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://philosophy.princeton.edu/content/paul-benacerraf-symposium|title=Paul Benacerraf Symposium {{!}} Department of Philosophy|website=philosophy.princeton.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-11-30|archive-date=2017-12-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171216011350/https://philosophy.princeton.edu/content/paul-benacerraf-symposium|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Benacerraf was born in [[Paris]] on 26 March 1930,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095458163|title=Paul Joseph Salomon Benacerraf - Oxford Reference|website=www.oxfordreference.com|language=en|access-date=2018-12-29|archive-date=2018-12-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181230044014/http://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095458163|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=AAAS /> to a Moroccan-Venezuelan [[Sephardic Jewish]] father, Abraham Benacerraf, and Algerian Jewish mother, Henrietta Lasry. In 1939 the family moved to [[Caracas]] and then to New York City.<ref name=":0">{{cite news|url=https://www.princeton.edu/pr/pwb/98/1123/benacer.htm|title=Whatever I am now, it happened here|last=Moseley|first=Caroline|date=November 23, 1998|work=Princeton Weekly Bulletin|access-date=October 13, 2011|publisher=Princeton University|archive-date=February 14, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120214081849/http://www.princeton.edu/pr/pwb/98/1123/benacer.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

When the family returned to Caracas, Benacerraf remained in the United States, boarding at the [[Peddie School]] in [[Hightstown]], New Jersey. He attended [[Princeton University]] for both his undergraduate and graduate studies.<ref name=":0" />

He was elected a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1998.<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=June 2, 2011|archive-date=June 18, 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060618085806/http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Benacerraf died on 13 January 2025, at the age of 94.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sigsbee |first=Dustin |date=2025-01-16 |title=Paul Benacerraf (1930–2025) - Daily Nous |url=https://dailynous.com/2025/01/16/paul-benacerraf-1930-2025/ |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=dailynous.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2025/02/06/paul-benacerraf-preeminent-philosopher-mathematics-princeton-alumnus-and-life/|title= Paul Benacerraf, preeminent philosopher of mathematics, Princeton alumnus and 'life-changing teacher,' dies at 93|date=2025-02-06|publisher =[[Princeton University]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://centraljersey.com/2025/03/05/paul-joseph-salomon-benacerraf/|title=Paul Joseph Salomon Benacerraf|publisher=centraljersey.com}}</ref> His older brother was the Venezuelan [[Nobel Prize]]-winning immunologist [[Baruj Benacerraf]].

==Philosophical work<!--'Benacerraf's epistemological problem' redirects here-->==
Benacerraf was perhaps best known for his two papers "What Numbers Could Not Be" (1965) and "Mathematical Truth" (1973), and for his anthology on the philosophy of mathematics, co-edited with [[Hilary Putnam]].

In "What Numbers Could Not Be" (1965), Benacerraf argues against a [[Philosophy of mathematics#Platonism|Platonist]] view of mathematics, and for [[Mathematical structuralism|structuralism]], on the ground that what is important about numbers is the abstract structures they represent rather than the objects that number words ostensibly refer to.  In particular, this argument is based on the point that [[Ernst Zermelo]] and [[John von Neumann]] give distinct, and completely adequate, identifications of natural numbers with sets (see [[Zermelo ordinals]] and [[von Neumann ordinals]]). This argument is called [[Benacerraf's identification problem]].

In "Mathematical Truth" (1973), he argues that no interpretation of mathematics offers a satisfactory package of epistemology and semantics; it is possible to explain mathematical truth in a way that is consistent with our syntactico-semantical treatment of truth in non-mathematical language, and it is possible to explain our knowledge of mathematics in terms consistent with a causal account of epistemology, but it is in general not possible to accomplish both of these objectives simultaneously (this argument is called '''Benacerraf's epistemological problem'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA-->). He argues for this on the grounds that an adequate account of truth in mathematics implies the existence of abstract mathematical objects, but that such objects are epistemologically inaccessible because they are causally inert and beyond the reach of sense perception. On the other hand, an adequate epistemology of mathematics, say one that ties truth-conditions to proof in some way, precludes understanding how and why the truth-conditions have any bearing on truth.

*Benacerraf, Paul (1960) ''Logicism, Some Considerations'', Princeton, Ph.D. Dissertation, University Microfilms.
*———— (1965) "What Numbers Could Not Be", ''The Philosophical Review'', 74:47–73.
*———— (1967) [https://web.archive.org/web/20040806120644/http://www.univ.trieste.it/~etica/2003_1/3_monographica.htm "God, the Devil, and Gödel"], ''The Monist'', 51: 9–33.
*———— (1973) "Mathematical Truth", ''The Journal of Philosophy'', 70: 661–679.
*———— (1981) "Frege: The Last Logicist", ''The Foundations of Analytic Philosophy'', ''Midwest Studies in Philosophy'', 6: 17–35.
*———— (1985) "Skolem and the Skeptic", ''Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society'', Supplementary Volume 56: 85–115.
*———— and Putnam, Hilary (eds.) (1983) ''Philosophy of Mathematics : Selected Readings'' 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press: New York.
*———— (1996) "Recantation or Any old ω-sequence would do after all", ''Philosophia Mathematica'', 4: 184–189.
*———— (1996) ''What Mathematical Truth Could Not Be – I'', in ''Benacerraf and His Critics'', A. Morton and S. P. Stich, eds., Blackwell's, Oxford and Cambridge, pp 9–59.
*———— (1999) ''What Mathematical Truth Could Not Be – II'', in ''Sets and Proofs'', S. B. Cooper and [[John Truss|J. K. Truss]], eds., Cambridge University Press, pp.&nbsp;27–51.
